newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire governor says main goal to avert violence.
newsitem.headline: Zaire governor says main goal to avert violence.

text.p: The leader of Zaire's Shaba province said in a speech on Saturday that his main goal was to avert bloodshed, a message many locals saw as a sign that advancing rebels would meet little resistance.

Kyungu wa Kumwanza, new governor of the region he calls by its old name Katanga, told a rally of some 5,000 supporters in Zaire's nervous second city of Lubumbashi that he would act ruthlessly against anyone who tried to loot it.
"Anyone seen carrying a television away on his head will go to meet the Lord with that television," Kyungu bellowed.
"Katanga refuses to destroy itself, or to destroy its people and belongings," he said. "We must not have bloodshed, we want liberty for all."
Laurent Kabila's rebels are slowly closing in on Lubumbashi, capital of the copper-rich province in Zaire's far southeast near the Zambian border.
On Friday and Saturday they entered the diamond mining centre of Mbuji-Mayi in next-door Kasai province, leaving Lubumbashi as the obvious next target. They are at most 220 km (135 miles) away.
Using vague turns of speech, Kyungu said he had called on army commanders to avoid bloodshed and looting and said their mission was to protect citizens and their belongings.
Without once mentioning the rebels by name, he said that if people were expecting someone to arrive, they should await him calmly in their homes rather than fleeing.
"He's a very, very clever man," said Kaizer Nzenga, a waiter. "By saying he does not want fighting in his region, he is asking the people to let Kabila come in freely."
Others in the crowd echoed Nzenga's remarks, but said they were still unsure how the several hundred troops in Lubumbashi, with nowhere left to flee to, would react.

Local hopes that the army would give up on Lubumbashi, deciding it was hopeless to try to defend it, were dealt a blow with the news that a planeload of reinforcements from the capital Kinshasa had arrived.
In Mbuji-Mayi and elsewhere, retreating Zairean soldiers looted as they fled and local youths then joined in.
Lubumbashi -- where some people openly cheered "Kabila, Kabila" after Kyungu's rally -- fears it may share a similar fate.

The populist Kyungu, trying to hold onto his support as Kabila, also a Katangan, comes closer, used the rally to tell the city's million residents he would prevent looting and do all he could to improve their sorry economic lot.
The crowd in Lubumbashi's main Moise Tshombe square, named by Kyungu after an earlier separatist leader, was by local standards moderate in size and enthusiasm.
Kyungu promised to halt the sinking exchange rate to the dollar in Shaba, which uses banknotes shunned by the rest of Zaire that have become a de facto separate currency.

The potentially rich region has been impoverished by corruption and mismanagement during more than three decades of rule by President Mobutu Sese Seko, whose envoy was meeting Kabila's representatives for peace talks as the rally was held.

Expatriates in Lubumbashi, many of whom own businesses and have much to fear from looting, have mostly sent their families away but some 300 remain, most of them Belgians. Belgium is sending five soldiers to the city to help protect them.
Mobutu suspended Kyungu in 1995 after he openly called for secession for Shaba, but reinstated him two weeks ago in a move widely seen as a classic Mobutu bid to divide the loyalty of his opponents.
